item.title: The path from brain to words is rerouted in opioid addiction
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Whether spontaneous speech preserves how the brain encoded an experience is unknown. We tested this question in opioid use disorder (OUD), in which drug cues outweigh other rewards. Eighty-two people with OUD and 34 controls watched the opening of the film Trainspotting during functional magnetic resonance imaging, then retold it in their own words. Language-model analyses showed that people with OUD dwelt on craving, personal identification and recovery, devoting more of their retelling to drug scenes. In 65 participants with imaging, this speech bias tracked how strongly the brain had distinguished drug from non-drug scenes during viewing, in left frontoparietal cortex in controls but left temporal cortex in OUD. Direct comparison showed left accumbens coupling positive in OUD and negative in controls, and left superior frontal coupling weaker in OUD. Spontaneous speech thus carries a trace of neural encoding whose route depends on what the experience meant to the speaker.

item.title: Beyond reduced alpha power: a weaker temporal link between alpha and other brain rhythms in Alzheimer's disease
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Reduced alpha power is among the most consistently reported resting electroencephalography (EEG) features of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, alpha activity also interacts with other rhythms over time, a dynamic aspect that power measures do not capture. Whether AD weakens this temporal interaction, and whether such a change carries information beyond reduced alpha power, remains unclear. Methods: We analyzed public eyes-closed resting EEG from 29 healthy controls (HC), 36 patients with AD and 23 with frontotemporal dementia (FTD). After separating periodic from aperiodic activity, we tracked the aperiodic exponent and periodic theta, alpha, beta and gamma activity in consecutive 1-s windows. A vector autoregressive model predicted these five measures from the preceding window. Alpha's predictive contribution (Gα) was the increase in prediction error for theta, beta and gamma when the model was refitted without alpha as a predictor, with training and testing on separate time blocks of each recording. AD-HC differences were adjusted for age and sex, then for alpha expression (periodic alpha power) and signal quality (dynamic range and spatial reliability), with alpha self-persistence (alpha's carry-over between windows) as a benchmark. We also tested whether expression and Gα each added information about AD beyond the other. An exploratory Jansen-Rit-family circuit model examined whether expression and Gα can change partly independently. Results: Gα was lower in AD than in HC (adjusted difference in 10^3Gα, -3.19; 95% confidence interval -5.25 to -1.13; p = 0.0035), with a consistent direction across sensitivity analyses. Adjustment for alpha expression and signal quality retained 75.8% of this difference but only 4.4% of the self-persistence difference. Expression and Gα each added information beyond the other (Holm-adjusted p = 0.012 for both). FTD contrasts were inconclusive. In the circuit model, reducing local recurrent excitation lowered alpha expression without an estimated decrease in Gα, whereas reducing downstream input lowered Gα with a smaller change in expression. Conclusions: At the group level, the resting alpha abnormality in AD comprises two partly nonredundant dimensions: reduced expression and a weaker temporal link between alpha and subsequent multi-rhythm activity. Quantifying this temporal link may complement conventional spectral markers of AD.

item.title: From micro-architecture to networks: canonical neurobiological architecture of functional brain organization across the lifespan and in psychopathology
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Understanding how macroscale functional network connectivity (FNC) across the lifespan and in psychopathology is spatially organized with respect to microscale neurobiological architecture remains a challenge. Here, we constructed a cross-omics mapping framework by linking resting-state fMRI data (5,349 individuals, 6-80 years) with 49 neurobiological markers (24 cell types, 19 neurotransmitters, 6 mitochondria). We show that FNC development and aging unfold along cellular and molecular gradients. Specifically, spatial correspondence between age-related FNC changes and neurobiological microprofile networks varied by life stage, peaking for cell types in adolescence, neurotransmitter systems in mid-young adulthood and mitochondrial phenotypes in early adulthood. Applying normative modeling to 5 psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, autism, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), we identified disorder-specific and cross-disorder FNC phenotypes spatially associated with neurobiological architecture. Together, these findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework linking functional brain organization and dysfunction to canonical neurobiological architecture across the lifespan and psychiatric disorders.

item.title: Whole-brain normative modeling across multiple functional connectivity metrics in MEG
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Normative modeling has recently emerged in structural and functional neuroimaging as a promising approach to characterize neuropathology at the individual level. Trained on large healthy cohorts, these models predict expected measurements from covariates such as age and sex while quantifying normal population variability. Individual measurements can then be compared against the model to identify deviations associated with pathology. While most normative models of brain function have been based on functional MRI, EEG and MEG offer more direct measurements of brain activity at higher temporal resolution. Despite the promise, how to adequately perform normative modelling at the whole-brain level on these modalities remains challenging. We here propose M/EEG-FUNCOIN to identify age- and sex-related dimensions of change in functional connectivity from a plethora of FC measures from electrophysiology: amplitude envelope correlation, phase-locking value, and time-delay embedding covariance. Using resting-state MEG data from the Cambridge Centre for Aging and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) dataset, we show that M/EEG-FUNCOIN can: (i) characterize age- and sex-related whole-brain functional connectivity patterns in greater detail than existing methods; and (ii) effectively capture meaningful deviations in connectivity in individuals that rank high and low in cognitive ability. Altogether, these results show great potential for applications in complex, network-level brain pathology.

item.title: Functional and Structural Brain Age Gaps as Complementary Predictive Markers for Cognitive Performance
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Cognitive decline is characterized by substantial inter-individual variability across the lifespan, even among clinically healthy adults. However, it is unclear how structural and functional brain organization jointly relate to differences in cognitive performance within the typical populations. We considered a multimodal brain age framework by predicting for each subject its age from either structural MRI or resting-state functional MRI, after training on the 1000BRAINS cohort (901 participants, 18-85 years). Following, a structural and a functional brain age gap markers were defined as the deviations with respect to the real chronological age. We then used the markers to characterize the interplay between structure and function in shaping cognitive performances. Our findings reveal that the functional marker is as important to predict global cognitive performance as the structural marker. The most accurate prediction was found for global cognition, executive functions and episodic memory, followed by working memory, attention and language. In particular, the structural marker was contributing to all domains, except for working memory, whereas the functional marker had the highest contribution. Overall, structural and functional brain age models together provide a meaningful subject-level summary of brain information for predicting cognition, supporting a multidimensional view of typical aging.

item.title: Resting-state alpha scale-free dynamics predict individual differences in the balance between reward-learned and preference-based values during free choice
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Values learned through reward can continue to influence choices guided by one's own preferences, such as which painting to hang, to an extent that varies across individuals. Because such preferences build up gradually across choices, their expression may depend on how well internally generated states are sustained over time, a property indexed by long-range temporal correlations (LRTC) in intrinsic brain activity. We tested whether resting-state alpha-band LRTC predicts individual differences in the balance between reward-learned and preference-based values. Eighty-one participants learned through probabilistic feedback which of four abstract shapes tended to be rewarded, and then judged their preferences among these shapes and 11 new shapes without feedback. Alpha LRTC was estimated by detrended fluctuation analysis of resting-state electroencephalography recorded before, between, and after the tasks. A trial-level mixed-effects model showed that reward history influenced preference judgments and that this influence decreased with resting-state alpha LRTC: participants with weak LRTC chose high-reward shapes over new shapes on 75% of trials, whereas those with strong LRTC were close to indifference (54%). The relationship was distributed across the scalp, stable across recordings, and not explained by spectral power or learning performance. Resting-state alpha LRTC is thus related to how strongly reward-learned values are carried into preference-based choice. Given the view that stronger LRTC reflects a longer window over which internally generated states are integrated, the observed relationship could arise because the window is biased toward values built up through one's own choices, or because it attenuates values learned under a criterion that no longer applies; which account holds remains to be determined.

item.title: Cellular and mitochondrial correlates of regional glucose metabolism in the human cortex
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Regional differences in human brain glucose metabolism reflect local energy demands, but their cellular and mitochondrial determinants remain unclear. We combined [18F]FDG positron emission tomography in healthy human participants with estimates of cellular composition and mitochondrial density to unravel (sub)cellular correlates of heterogeneity in brain glucose metabolism. By correcting for RNA content and differential gene expression due to postmortem sampling, we addressed methodological shortcomings in multimodal neuroimaging integration. We introduce transcriptionally derived cytoarchitectonic maps of the human cortex that are consistent with histological findings, providing a biologically grounded framework for relating in vivo neuroimaging signals. Accordingly, mitochondrial distribution showed strong association with the intrinsic energy requirements at resting state. In contrast, relations between metabolism and neuronal composition were driven by sensory input and mitochondria-sparse thin-axon neurons, suggesting that stimulation-induced energy demand is met rather by neuronal processes that are independent of mitochondrial abundance to maintain efficient information processing.

item.title: Brain synchrony between interacting sibling pairs during real-time cooperation: an fMRI hyperscanning study
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Siblings typically represent the longest-lasting social relationships. Second-person neuroscience provides a framework for studying the neural mechanisms of real-time, reciprocal social interactions. Yet, most studies have focused on simplified coordination tasks, limited brain regions, and did not investigate neural dynamics between siblings. In the first study investigating brain synchrony between siblings to date, we used fMRI hyperscanning to simultaneously record brain activity in 50 same-sex healthy young adult sibling pairs while they played a complex collaborative problem-solving Tetris game requiring continuous non-verbal complementary coordination. Brain synchrony was quantified using inter-subject correlation across 36 regions of interest (ROIs) of the social brain atlas. The interacting sibling pairs showed significantly higher brain synchrony than randomly permuted non-sibling pairs in 19 ROIs (FDR-corrected p < .05). These regions were primarily located within the higher-level theory of mind subnetwork (including bilateral temporo-parietal junction, precuneus and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex), and intermediate-level subnetwork (including anterior insula, inferior frontal gyrus). Greater synchrony in the left temporo-parietal junction significantly predicted better cooperative performance, suggesting that shared neural modelling of a partner's intentions supports effective collaboration. Synchrony in frontal and temporal regions was weakly modulated by cooperative and competitive sibling relationship characteristics; however, these effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons and should be interpreted cautiously (uncorr. p < .05). This study provides first evidence that real-time cooperation between siblings is supported by inter-brain synchrony in core social brain networks. We highlight the value of ecologically valid hyperscanning approaches for investigating neural mechanisms of cooperation in long-term relationships, advancing the field of relational neuroscience.

item.title: Resting-state functional brain changes in temporal lobe epilepsy with comorbid depression: A meta-analysis.
item.description:
Epilepsy & behavior : E&B
Objective To compare the differences in functional brain activity between patients with temporal lobe epilepsy comorbid with depressive disorder (TLE-D) and those with temporal lobe epilepsy without depressive disorder (TLE-ND) via a meta‑analysis of resting‑state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) studies, and to explore the functional brain activity features associated with depressive symptoms. Methods Systematic searches were conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Wanfang Data from database inception to September 2026 to identify cross-sectional studies comparing rs-fMRI-derived differences in functional brain activity between patients with temporal lobe epilepsy comorbid with depressive disorder (TLE-D) and those without depressive disorder (TLE-ND). Eligible rs-fMRI metrics included regional brain activity indices and functional connectivity indices. A meta-analysis of studies reporting regional brain activity indices was performed using anisotropic effect-size signed differential mapping (AES-SDM). Due to their limited number, studies reporting functional connectivity indices were only described narratively. Study selection and data extraction were then completed, and a voxel-based meta-analysis of the included studies was performed with AES-SDM. Results A total of six studies yielding nine datasets met the inclusion criteria, involving 100 patients with TLE-D and 108 patients with TLE-ND. Meta-analysis showed that, compared with the TLE-ND group, the TLE-D group had significantly increased spontaneous brain activity in the right precuneus, right angular gyrus, right superior frontal gyrus, left middle frontal gyrus, and left cerebellum (analyzed via AES-SDM with an initial exploratory threshold of uncorrected voxel-level P < 0.005 and cluster size ≥10 voxels, and validated by leave-one-out sensitivity analysis). No brain regions with significantly decreased spontaneous brain activity were detected. Conclusion These exploratory findings suggest that, compared with patients with TLE-ND, patients with TLE-D show distinct patterns of functional brain activity in multiple key nodes of the default mode network, including the precuneus and angular gyrus, as well as in prefrontal-related regions. These differences may provide preliminary neuroimaging evidence for understanding the neural mechanisms underlying depressive symptoms associated with temporal lobe epilepsy.

item.title: Global synchrony moderates sad mood and is associated with emotional Stroop interference and somatic symptoms.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Mood-congruent attention in depression has been studied via emotional interference tasks, including tasks comparing responses to sad and happy stimuli. Mood induction offers a way to experimentally induce sad mood in non-clinical samples and examine its association with subsequent emotional interference, including Sad-Happy interference. Previous studies have separately linked resting-state global neural dynamics (synchrony, metastability) to depressive symptoms and attentional processing. However, whether individual differences in baseline global synchrony and metastability relate to how individuals respond to sad mood remains largely unclear. This study therefore examined the relationship between neural dynamics, sadder mood after induction, and Sad-Happy interference. Depressive symptoms also encompass somatic domains alongside cognitive-affective domains, though these are rarely distinguished in neuroimaging studies. We further examined whether baseline neural dynamics and their association with sadder mood and Sad-Happy interference were related to depressive symptoms (total, cognitive-affective, and somatic). Forty-eight non-clinical individuals completed resting-state neuroimaging, mood induction (sad or non-sad), and an emotional Stroop task. We found in a cross-sectional moderated mediation model that sadder mood after induction was associated with greater interference from sad compared to happy stimuli at medium and high levels of global synchrony, particularly in exploratory path models that included somatic symptoms. Findings suggest that individual differences in resting-state global synchrony may be a neural correlate of sadder mood after induction and Sad-Happy interference in non-clinical individuals. This study offers preliminary associations linking neural dynamics, sad mood, emotional interference, and somatic symptoms, providing insights into the role of neural dynamics in emotional and attentional processing.

item.title: Age and sex impact resting-state EEG aperiodic activity beyond symptom associations in persistent post-concussive symptoms
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Objective: to investigate whether resting-state EEG aperiodic parameters (i.e., offset and exponent) are associated with symptom burden and demographic factors in patients with persistent post-concussive symptoms (PPCS) and differ from healthy controls. Methods: In this cross-sectional observational study, resting-state eye-closed high-density EEG was recorded in patients with PPCS and in age-matched healthy controls. Aperiodic parameters were extracted from EEG power spectra. In patients, hierarchical multiple linear regression models included age and sex as a base model, with additional demographic and clinical symptoms entered separately. Patient-control differences were assessed using multiple linear regression adjusted for age and sex. Results: Seventy patients with PPCS (54 female; 39.57 ±12.21 y.; 109.5 [76.5; 196] days post-concussion) recruited from a concussion care pathway and 38 healthy controls (17 female; 39.61± 13.57 y.) were included. In patients, younger age and male sex were associated with higher offset and exponent values (all p under .014). None of the additional demographic and clinical variables improved model fit beyond age and sex (all p under.143). After adjustment for age and sex, neither offset (p=.898) nor exponent (p=.100) differed between patients and controls. Conclusion: Resting-state aperiodic EEG parameters were consistently associated with age and sex, but not with self-reported symptom burden or clinical characteristics in patients with PPCS. Not accounting for these factors may generate apparent group differences attributable, at least in part, to demographic variability. Significance: Age and sex are important sources of inter-individual variability in resting-state aperiodic EEG activity and should be systematically considered when investigating such features.

item.title: Post-Learning Reactivation of Memories for Naturalistic Continuous Experiences
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Memories are not static records of the past; rather, the act of remembering can change how an event is recalled. Intriguingly, several studies also suggest that memories may be reactivated during rest. However, reactivation has largely been studied for spatial tasks and discrete stimuli, and we know little about whether spontaneous reactivation occurs for long timescale naturalistic events and how reactivation affects retention. Using fMRI, we show that neural activity patterns in the hippocampus and the Default Mode Network during encoding of narrative events were spontaneously reactivated during rest. Contrary to predictions, reactivation did not strengthen recall of movie details, and instead exploratory analyses suggested that reactivation in the hippocampus was associated with more gist-like recall one week later. These findings support the idea that memories for complex events may be spontaneously reactivated, but they suggest that rather than simply strengthening episodic memories, reactivation might help transform them.

item.title: Longitudinal fMRI reveals altered developmental trajectories of functional network organisation associated with adolescent cannabis use
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Adolescence is a critical period of brain development during which the endocannabinoid system continues to mature. These developmental changes may contribute to age-related differences in the association between cannabis use and large-scale functional network organisation, yet this association remains incompletely characterised. We hypothesised that regular cannabis use would be associated with differential one-year changes in resting-state functional connectivity between adolescents and adults. Resting-state fMRI data at two time points, one year apart, were analysed from 66 participants (31 aged 16-17 years; 35 aged 26-29 years) including 29 with regular cannabis use and 37 age-matched cannabis-naive controls. Seed-to-voxel analyses examined longitudinal changes in functional connectivity across age and cannabis-use groups. Year change, age by user-group interactions were identified in salience and default mode network connectivity, including divergent changes in anticorrelations with medial prefrontal, thalamic, cerebellar and juxtapositional regions. Directionality of effects differed by network and region. Additional main effects of user group were observed for executive control and associative striatal connectivity, with the cannabis-use group showing decreased positive connectivity and reduced anticorrelation, respectively. Changes in functional connectivity were developmentally dissociable and predominantly observed in regions contributing to attentional and transmodal processing. These findings suggest that cannabis may be associated with alterations in the maturational refinement of higher-order neural systems, potentially reflecting age-related differences in neurobiological sensitivity to cannabis exposure. Considering developmental stage may therefore be important for characterising cannabis-related neurobiological differences and may have implications for understanding age-dependent vulnerability to cannabis-related psychiatric outcomes.

item.title: Action features dominate cortical representation during natural vision.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Cortical resources are allocated into systems specialized for processing ecologically relevant features of the world. These features are typically studied in isolation using controlled experimental stimuli, making it difficult to assess the relative importance of different kinds of features that tend to overlap during natural vision. In the current study, we evaluated the relative contributions of action, agent, and scene features in predicting cortical activity while participants viewed a 1-h nature documentary. We tested four sets of model features: semantic vectors capturing the observed action, agent, and scene features derived from an annotation of the stimulus, as well as low-level visual motion-energy features. We used banded ridge regression to fit vertex-wise encoding models from the combination of all four sets of features. While each set of features predicted neural activity in the expected areas, the action features predicted more widespread activity. A variance partitioning analysis revealed that the action features captured the most unique variance in neural activity across a much larger extent of cortex than the agent or scene features. Our findings suggest that cortical activity during dynamic, natural vision is dominated by features for understanding the actions of others.

item.title: Decoding individual differences in mental information from human brain responses predicted by deep neural networks.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Brain decoding using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has high potential for evaluating unobservable mental information that varies across individuals in everyday situations. Although estimating individual differences in mental information using brain decoding could be effective for social applications, especially in neuromarketing, the physical constraints and high costs of fMRI limit the practical application in real-world settings. To overcome these limitations, we propose a framework to estimate individual differences in decodable mental information using brain responses predicted by deep neural networks (DNNs). In this framework, DNN-based models are trained to predict fMRI responses to natural movie scenes. Then, additional fMRI measurements are no longer required because mental information for new movie scenes can be decoded from the predicted responses instead of the measured ones. A large-scale analysis revealed that the proposed predicted-response decoding captures individual difference patterns consistent with those derived from conventional measured-response decoding across various cognitive domains. Of the 88 cognitive labels associated with movie scenes, individual difference patterns could be captured for more than 70% of the labels. This framework offers a promising approach for evaluating personal mental information with substantially reduced reliance on fMRI, thereby expanding the potential for social applications of brain decoding.

item.title: Insular subregional dysfunction in panic disorder: A multimodal MRI study.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Background The spatial organization of insular abnormalities across connectional-architecture-defined subregions in panic disorder (PD) remains unclear. We examined structural and resting-state functional measures using the Brainnetome Atlas. Methods Forty-nine medication-naïve patients with PD and Fifty healthy controls underwent structural and resting-state MRI. Gray matter volume (GMV), amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (ALFF), and regional homogeneity (ReHo) were assessed across six insular subregions. Four prespecified functional connections were examined, together with exploratory Granger causality analysis between dIg and S1 and an AAL3 whole-insula comparison. Results dIg-S1 functional connectivity was reduced in PD (β = -0.148, 95% CI [-0.248, -0.048], pFDR = 0.017). ALFF showed a Group × Subregion interaction (F(5,578) = 4.162, p = 0.001). Only the ventral agranular insula (vIa) showed significantly higher ALFF after false discovery rate (FDR) correction (pFDR = 0.016), with a larger group effect than other subregions. The interaction persisted after temporal signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) adjustment (F(5,577) = 2.582, p = 0.025), but the vIa-specific effect was nonsignificant in a separate vIa-only tSNR-adjusted model (p = 0.194). ReHo was directionally lower across all six subregions, but no contrast survived FDR correction. No robust subregional GMV differences or significant group differences in exploratory Granger causality were detected. Adjusted AAL3 whole-insula differences were nonsignificant. Conclusions PD showed measure-dependent insular functional alterations, including reduced dIg-S1 coupling and vIa-predominant ALFF differences, with the latter sensitive to signal quality and spatial smoothing.

item.title: Infant Negative Affect During Mother-Infant Interaction Is Associated with Neonatal Limbic-Prefrontal Connectivity in the First Month of Life.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
Background Early caregiving may shape neonatal limbic circuit organization, yet whether microanalytically coded interaction quality relates to neonatal limbic-prefrontal connectivity is unknown. We tested associations between infant and maternal affect during mother-infant interaction and neonatal limbic-prefrontal cortex (PFC) connectivity. Methods At approximately 30 days postnatal, 143 mother-infant dyads from the Healthy MiNDS cohort (São Paulo, Brazil) completed a video-recorded interaction coded with the Coding Interactive Behavior (CIB) system; infant negative affect was the percentage of interaction time in distress. Neonates underwent resting-state fMRI; limbic-PFC connectivity was quantified by principal component analysis of amygdala and hippocampus seed-to-ROI maps. Covariate-adjusted regressions tested associations. Results Infant negative affect was associated with right amygdala-PFC (β = -0.247, p = .003) and right hippocampus-PFC connectivity (β = -0.202, p = .021), both surviving FDR correction and robust across multiple analytic approaches. The amygdala association was limited to infant distress-related behaviors, whereas maternal positive expressiveness showed an independent, opposing association (β = 0.202, p = .019); no other CIB measure was significant. Exploratorily, connectivity was associated with sleep problems at 18-24 months in females (r = -.324, p = .030). Conclusions The emotional quality of early caregiving is associated with neonatal limbic circuit organization: infant distress is selectively associated with weaker amygdala-PFC connectivity, whereas maternal positive affect shows an independent opposing association. These findings identify the mother-infant relationship as a modifiable input to neonatal brain development.

item.title: Effects of dance and music training on the plasticity of the core empathy network: intra- and inter-network connectivity.
item.description:
PeerJ
Background Dance and music are two of the oldest and most universal forms of artistic expression, each requiring extensive training. Prolonged training is known to induce neuroplastic changes and enhance socio-emotional abilities such as empathy. The mirror neuron system (MNS) is associated with empathy; however, few studies systematically explored how dance and music training modulate the core empathy network, including subcortical regions within the limbic MNS. Method Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data were obtained from 25 dancers, 24 musicians and 39 demographically matched control group (both groups are healthy). Core regions within relevant brain networks, along with key subcortical components of limbic MNS, specifically the amygdala and basal ganglia, were defined as regions of interest (ROIs) to build a core empathy network. Graph-theoretical metrics, including within-network degree (WND) and between-network degree (BND), were calculated to evaluate connectivity patterns. These metrics were further correlated with empathy scores. Results Both dancers and musicians exhibited altered connectivity within the core empathy network. Dancers showed increased WND and BND between basal ganglia regions and the ventral attention network, whereas musicians demonstrated enhanced WND between the amygdala and the subcortical network. Notably, both groups exhibited reduced WND between the superior frontal gyrus and the sensorimotor network. The neural changes were correlated with Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI) empathy subscale scores, indicating training-related modulations in affective and cognitive empathy. Conclusion Dance and music training induce both distinct and overlapping patterns of neuroplasticity within the core empathy network that are associated with enhanced empathic ability. The findings support the potential of dance and music as systematic intervention programs.

item.title: Individual Differences in Sustained Attention Tune Semantic Abstraction in Neural Encoding of Narratives
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Neural encoding modeling for narrative comprehension -- using LLM embeddings to predict the temporal dynamics of neural activation -- is widely used to evaluate how well the brain represents certain semantic information. This approach, however, typically collapses semantic representation into a scalar fidelity score aggregated across participants, overlooking potentially rich individual differences and qualitative differences in naturalistic neural representations. In the current study, we addressed this gap by investigating how neural semantic encoding varies across individuals with sustained attention, and whether this difference is qualitative in addition to quantitative. Using fMRI data from 49 participants listening to an audiobook, Le Petit Prince, in English, we trained encoding models with GPT-2 embeddings at varying layers and forecasting lengths. Encoding models trained on high-level embeddings (from the 8th layer of GPT-2) showed significant brain-LLM alignment in 73 of 122 cortical and subcortical ROIs, concentrated in the temporal cortex and the default mode network. Functional connectivity strength in a validated connectome-based predictive model of sustained attention correlated with encoding performance in 18 ROIs, most strongly in the insula and in control and attention networks, with no ROI showing significant opposite relationship. Decomposing semantic information by levels of abstraction showed that the neural signature of sustained attention was selectively associated with a greater proportion of high-level gist information encoded in the frontoparietal and attention networks, while the opposite relationship emerged for proportion of low-level information. Sustained attention scores further predicted stronger predictive coding of upcoming narrative content across multiple networks across the whole brain (control, default mode, salience/ventral attention, limbic, and somatomotor networks). These findings suggest that sustained attention does not uniformly amplify neural semantic encoding, but instead shifts neural representations toward more compressed, gist-level formats that support anticipation of upcoming content. Individual differences in brain-LLM alignment can be a signature of representational strategy rather than noise, with potential utility for cognitive phenotyping.

item.title: Development of Neonatal Functional Brain Network Organisation and Its Association with Childhood Neurodevelopmental Outcomes
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The human brain undergoes rapid dynamic changes in the neonatal period that are essential for later cognitive and behavioural performance. Using resting-state fMRI data from 394 neonates (325 term-born, 69 preterm-born) within the first month after birth, we characterised the early development of functional network organisation, the effects of preterm birth, and the association between neonatal functional organisation and later neurodevelopmental outcomes in infancy (18 months) and childhood (4-6 years). We found increased functional integration and segregation across a wide range of functional sub-networks and increased mean functional connectivity strength (mean FCS) within the subcortical and cerebellar regions with increasing PMA at scan. Compared with term-born neonates, preterm-born neonates showed significantly lower mean FCS, functional integration and segregation globally. We further showed that whilst neonatal functional brain network organisation was not associated with neurodevelopmental outcomes measured during infancy (18 months), it was associated with later neurodevelopmental outcomes in early childhood (4-6 years). Specifically, higher functional integration and segregation at birth were linked with lower SDQ total difficulties score at 4-6 years. Our findings suggest that neonatal functional brain organisation reflects not only transient developmental processes, but also stable individual differences that provide insight into neurodevelopmental outcomes in later childhood.

item.title: Faster peak alpha frequency precedes higher menstrual pain in adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Brain differences in chronic pain are almost always measured after years of pain experience, leaving unresolved whether they create vulnerability to pain or result from it. Uniquely, menstrual pain has a developmentally scheduled onset (menarche, the first menstrual period), allowing the brain to be characterized before and after pain exposure occurs. Here we used longitudinal 64-channel EEG to measure resting brain activity in adolescents once before (n=250) and twice after (n=161, n=140) menarche. Before their first period, adolescents who later reported higher menstrual pain (30 or greater on a 0 to 100 VAS) already showed faster occipital peak alpha frequency compared to those who reported lower menstrual pain, a difference that persisted in the early (3 to 14 months) post-menarche time period. In contrast, oscillatory power and functional connectivity did not differ by menstrual pain group, suggesting that the widespread functional brain alterations reported in adults with painful periods take years to emerge. Peak alpha frequency increased, and theta power and connectivity decreased across the menarchal transition, consistent with typical adolescent maturation. However, longitudinal analyses stratified by higher and lower menstrual pain group suggested group specific timings for these neurodevelopmental changes. Overall, these findings suggest that early menstrual pain is not associated with widespread alterations in neural oscillations, but aspects of menstrual pain susceptibility may be reflected in resting peak alpha frequency. To our knowledge, this is the first neurophysiological trait shown to precede the onset of menstrual pain.

item.title: Frequency-Specific Cognitive Control Network Hypoconnectivity in Adolescents With Elevated Externalizing Symptoms
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Externalizing symptoms during adolescence are associated with behavioral difficulties and an increased risk of adverse developmental outcomes, and are often accompanied by difficulties in self-regulation across cognitive and emotional domains. Although prior neuroimaging studies have reported altered brain connectivity in externalizing psychopathology, most evidence comes from functional magnetic resonance imaging, leaving frequency-specific electrophysiological network dynamics poorly understood. We examined resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) functional connectivity in a community-based sample of 35 adolescents aged 13–15 years with relatively high or low parent-reported externalizing symptoms. Source-level connectivity was estimated using exact low-resolution electromagnetic tomography and lagged phase synchronization across delta-to-gamma frequency bands within the cognitive control network (CCN) and default mode network (DMN). Results Adolescents with higher externalizing symptoms showed reduced connectivity in five beta1- and gamma-band CCN connections, whereas no significant group differences were observed within the DMN. After adjustment for internalizing symptoms, bilateral anterior-insula connectivity in the beta1 band and left anterior insula–right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex connectivity in the gamma band remained significant. Lower left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex–right inferior frontal junction beta1 connectivity was also associated with greater self-reported physical aggression. Conclusions Elevated externalizing symptoms during adolescence may be linked to altered functional coordination within the cognitive control network. These findings highlight the potential value of frequency-resolved EEG connectivity for characterizing the neural correlates of adolescent externalizing symptoms.

item.title: Infra-slow brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions reveal a co-ordinated multisystem physiological network in humans.
item.description:
The Journal of physiology
Growing evidence indicates that brain continuously interacts with other physiological systems through neural and non-neural pathways. The brain-heart and brain-gut axes play a central role in homoeostasis, allostasis and behaviour, but also in cognitive aspects, including emotion and decision-making. Disruptions in these axes have been linked to a wide range of cardiovascular, neurological and psychiatric disorders. Despite this evidence, triadic crosstalk between the brain, heart and gut remains largely unexplored. Brain activity, cardiac autonomic fluctuations and gastric rhythms all exhibit slow temporal components in resting state, suggesting that brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions may occur over time scales from the infra-slow (0.01-0.1 Hz) physiological range. Using open-access electrophysiological recordings from 28 healthy subjects at rest, we extracted time-varying power dynamics describing the activity of the three organs: brain alpha power, cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic indices, and the power of the gastric rhythm. Statistical associations among these organs were quantified using the maximal information coefficient across the extended temporal delay range. Physiological interactions were confirmed using surrogate-based testing, which allowed us to construct the network topology of interactions between the three organs. Our findings show that triadic brain-heart-gut interactions form a multidirectional network primarily at infra-slow time scales during resting state. This study offers one of the first insights into the physiology of brain-heart-gut interplay, providing a methodological baseline for the development of more comprehensive biomarkers based on network dynamics capable of linking pathological conditions to dysregulation across multiple organ systems. KEY POINTS: First in-human, non-invasive investigation of parallel brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions in awake, healthy subjects. We analysed simultaneous electroencephalographic (EEG), electrocardiographic (ECG) and electrogastrographic (EGG) recordings and quantified strength and temporal scale of the derived time series associations to construct a large-scale network of interactions. We found that brain-heart-gut interactions extend into the infra-slow range (0.01-0.1 Hz), indicating that spontaneous fluctuations in the electrophysiological activity of one organ at rest are typically followed by corresponding changes in the other two. We consistently found a robust brain-heart-gut network topology across subjects, with multidirectional interactions and bodily dynamics converging towards midline central-posterior EEG regions. These findings provide one of the first endeavours in characterizing the physiology of brain-heart-gut interactions and a methodology with strong biomarker development potential.

item.title: Gamma-band network segregation links corollary discharge dysfunction and anomalous self-experiences in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Schizophrenia research
Anomalous self-experiences (ASEs) are a core feature of psychotic disorders and reflect disturbances in ipseity. Impairments in corollary discharge mechanism have been proposed as a neurobiological substrate of ASEs, and an imbalance between brain network integration and segregation, may impair the coherent flow of mental contents, thereby disrupting their fluid and implicit character. However, the relationship between corollary discharge and functional network properties has not been directly examined. This link was assessed in thirty participants with schizophrenia and thirty healthy controls. Functional network was computed using the Phase Locking Value (PLV) from resting-state EEG in the gamma band and two parameters were calculated: the clustering coefficient (ClC, as a proxy for segregation) and the path length (PL, as a proxy for integration); corollary discharge was indexed by N1 suppression in a talk-listen paradigm; and ASEs were evaluated using the 'Inventory of Psychotic-Like Anomalous Self-Experiences' (IPASE) total score. Patients with schizophrenia showed significantly greater gamma-band network segregation and lower integration than healthy controls. Moreover, higher segregation in this band was associated with reduced N1 suppression and greater ASEs severity in patients, whereas network integration was not associated with N1 suppression nor ASEs. These findings suggest that excessive gamma-band network segregation may be correlated with disrupted corollary discharge functioning and may compromise the distinction between self-generated and external stimuli. Therefore, it may alter the sense of ipseity by interfering with the integration of mental contents into the flow of consciousness, thereby contributing to greater severity of ASEs.

item.title: Reduced short-lag autoregressive carry-over in resting-state latent dynamics in major depressive disorder.
item.description:
Psychiatry research. Neuroimaging
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is increasingly characterized as a disorder of brain dynamics, but the temporal scale on which resting-state activity differs from healthy controls remains unclear. We analyzed resting-state fMRI data from 71 participants (51 MDD, 20 controls; OpenNeuro ds002748) using bilateral grid-extracted left-right difference signals projected into a control-defined latent space. Across 30 analysis configurations spanning five denoising pipelines, three latent dimensionalities, and two left-right correction settings, MDD showed reduced mean lag-1 autocorrelation in 24 of 30 configurations (integrated β = -0.0321, p = 0.036) and reduced AR(1) gain φ in 24 of 30 (β = -0.0316, p = 0.037), both robust to adjustment for pipeline, age, sex, and head motion. The broader autocorrelation area under lags 1-10 was not significantly reduced (β = -0.0099, p = 0.22), and lag-by-lag analysis localized the group difference specifically to lag 1. A model-comparison analysis identified AR-gain reduction as one of three competing candidate generative transformations rather than the unique winner. MDD is thus associated with a focal short-lag autoregressive carry-over reduction, a candidate latent-dynamical phenotype rather than a fully identified mechanism.

item.title: Left Temporoparietal Neural Synchrony Tracks Cooperative Performance Across Adult Dyads
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Cooperation requires interacting individuals to coordinate their actions toward shared goals, and interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) has been proposed as a neural correlate of this coordination. However, the relationship between INS and cooperative performance remains heterogeneous, and relatively little is known about how it varies across social relationships. The present study examined INS and behavioral performance during a naturalistic cooperative tabletop Jenga task in close-friend, romantic-partner, and mother–child dyads (N = 284 participants). Brain activity was simultaneously recorded using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning, and INS was quantified using wavelet transform coherence across the bilateral inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and temporoparietal junction (TPJ). Cooperative performance was assessed using tower collapse and the number of valid turns completed during the game. True interacting dyads exhibited significantly greater neural synchrony than surrogate dyads across all examined regional pairings ( d range = 0.35–0.55), indicating robust interaction-related inter-brain synchrony. Behavioral performance was not associated with INS at the whole-network level. Region-specific analyses, however, showed that tower collapse was associated with reduced synchrony in the left TPJ–left TPJ ( p Bonf = 0.009) and left TPJ–right TPJ ( p Bonf = 0.017) pairings, whereas the number of valid turns was unrelated to INS. Follow-up analyses further indicated that the association between tower collapse and left TPJ–left TPJ synchrony was present in close-friend ( p Bonf = 0.020) and romantic-partner ( p Bonf = 0.026) dyads but not in mother–child dyads. These findings suggest that the behavioral relevance of interpersonal neural synchrony is not uniform, but depends on the neural systems involved, the specific index of cooperative performance, and the relational and developmental context in which interaction unfolds.

item.title: Accentuated Divergence, Constrained Expression: Autistic Traits Modulate the Creative Brain in Adults with ADHD
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition, and co-occurring autistic traits may shape its phenotypic expression. Although creativity has been discussed as a relative strength in ADHD, it remains unclear whether autistic traits are associated with different dimensions of creativity in adults with ADHD and whether large-scale brain networks contribute to these associations. Methods We compared divergent thinking (DT) and real-life creativity between 65 adults with ADHD and 73 neurotypical controls. We used subgroup comparisons, partial correlation analyses, and multiple regression models to determine the effects of autistic traits (ATs) on creativity dimensions within the ADHD cohort. Guided by prior creativity-network research, we analyzed resting-state functional connectivity (FC) of the Default Mode Network (DMN) and Frontoparietal Network (FPN) to uncover the neural mechanisms. Results The ADHD cohort demonstrated significantly higher scores on both DT ( p s = 0.002–0.009) and real-life creativity measures ( p s = 0.011–0.017) compared to the neurotypical control group. Importantly, increased ATs within the ADHD group were associated with a dissociated creativity profile, showing positive associations with DT but negative associations with real-life creativity. At the neural level, stronger right DMN–FPN connectivity mediated positive associations between ATs and DT performance (ps = 0.007–0.018), but mediated a negative association between ATs and self-reported imagination (p = 0.029). Conclusions In individuals with ADHD, co-occurring ATs exert a paradoxical effect on creativity, enhancing DT while compromising real-life creative achievement. In this subgroup with ADHD and elevated ATs, interventions should capitalize on ATs-associated ideational strengths while circumventing translational barriers, to enhance real-world creative outcomes.

item.title: Predicting upcoming visual features during eye movements yields scene representations aligned with human visual cortex.
item.description:
Science advances
Natural scenes are complex arrangements of objects, surfaces, and backgrounds. For the brain's visual system to effectively operate, it needs to extract not only what objects are present but also their spatial and semantic relations. We hypothesize that such structures may be learned, in a self-supervised fashion, by exploiting temporal regularities of natural active vision: Each fixation reveals a glimpse that is related to the previous one via co-occurrence and saccade-conditioned spatial regularities. We instantiate this idea with glimpse prediction networks (GPNs), recurrent models trained to predict the embedding of the next glimpse along human-like scanpaths. GPNs are shown to successfully extract complex scene information, including object co-occurrences and spatial object arrangements, and integrate information across glimpses. GPN representations align strongly with human fMRI responses in mid- and higher-level visual cortex and match, often outperform, alternative state-of-the-art ANN models, establishing next-glimpse-prediction as a biologically plausible route toward brain-aligned scene representations.

item.title: EEG Edge-Centric Dynamics Reveal Distinct Post-Stroke Somatosensory Network Responses to Vibratory and Electrical Stimulation.
item.description:
IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics
Stroke-induced somatosensory deficits disrupt sensorimotor integration (SMI) and limit motor recovery, yet the immediate network-level effects of different somatosensory interventions remain unclear, hindering patient-specific rehabilitation planning. We propose an informatics framework based on edge-centric dynamic connectivity (ECDC) to characterize transient, whole-brain EEG network responses to sensory-level focal vibratory stimulation (FVS) and neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES). We analyzed EEG recordings from 15 chronic stroke participants and 15 healthy controls during forearm stimulation and quantified temporal network dynamics, spectral network organization, and interhemispheric interactions from instantaneous overlapping functional networks. Compared with NMES, FVS in stroke participants induced a distinct neurophysiological profile, including (i) shorter global theta-network latency, suggesting faster attentional engagement; (ii) higher contralesional alpha network diversity, indicating enhanced somatosensory recruitment; and (iii) reduced theta-alpha phase-amplitude coupling, reflecting decoupled interhemispheric interactions that may support adaptive reorganization. These findings provide interpretable network signatures for differentiating stimulation-specific brain responses and suggest a data driven route toward personalized SMI rehabilitation.

item.title: Naturalistic spatial education engages distinct neural processes for mental rotation, cognitive load, and linguistic demands.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Neuroscience studies typically isolate spatial cognition using simplified tasks targeting a single cognitive process. However, during formal spatial education, the brain rarely performs one cognitive operation at a time. Here, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to assess neural systems involved in dynamically processing an educational spatial visualization lesson. We quantified lesson content using an instructional-design framework capturing variation in spatial complexity, cognitive load, and verbal density. We then characterized how instructional demands modulated brain function using content-evoked responses, functional connectivity, and network-centrality. Spatial transformations during instruction robustly recruited parietal and premotor regions, which were linearly modulated by spatial complexity. This parietal dominance aligns with theories that these areas encode geometric and quantitative dimensions. In contrast, domain-general frontal activity tracked overall processing demands, and language regions tracked verbal density. Activity also varied with learners' spatial abilities: higher spatial performers showed stronger modulation of parietal and premotor regions as spatial demands increased, and greater domain-general modulation across content types. Thus, the same circuitry representing spatial transformations during instruction also reflects individual variation in spatial cognition. Parietal regions showed the highest centrality and strongest within-network coherence, marking them as the central hub of the system, and distinguishing them from less central and less coherent domain-general regions. Together, the findings reveal how the brain dynamically decomposes complex spatial instruction, preserving parietal-centered spatial processing, while coordinating support from premotor, domain-general, and language systems. These findings begin to reveal how spatial cognition operates within the complexity of formal instruction.

item.title: Thalamocortical dysconnectivity shapes cortical hierarchy disruption across illness durations in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Background Schizophrenia is increasingly conceptualized as a disorder of circuit-level dysfunction. However, how thalamocortical abnormalities differ across cohorts with varying illness durations and relate to large-scale cortical hierarchical organization remains unclear. Methods We analyzed resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 1,223 patients with schizophrenia and 1,224 matched healthy controls across 12 datasets. The datasets were grouped as early-, middle-, and late-stage cohorts. Connectivity gradient mapping was applied to characterize thalamocortical organization, and computational modeling evaluated simulated hierarchical changes after modifying thalamic-salience connectivity. Results We identified a schizophrenia-relevant sensorimotor-salience-association axis that captures systematic differences in thalamocortical abnormality profiles across the stage cohorts. Along this axis, case-control effects in association regions were positive in the early-stage cohort but negative in the middle- and late-stage cohorts, whereas sensorimotor regions showed the converse pattern. This cross-cohort pattern was accompanied by reduced cortical hierarchical separation in cohorts with longer illness duration. In contrast, salience-related thalamic regions showed negative case-control effects in all three stage cohorts, with larger effect sizes in the middle- and late-stage cohorts, and these alterations were associated with clinical symptoms. Computational modification of thalamic-salience connectivity increased simulated cortical hierarchical differentiation, particularly in the middle-stage cohort. Conclusions These findings indicate that thalamocortical dysconnectivity, centered on disrupted thalamic-salience interactions, is associated with systematic differences in cortical hierarchical organization across cohorts. The cross-cohort pattern of salience-related abnormalities highlights thalamic-salience coupling as a circuit-level link to cortical hierarchical differentiation and a candidate for future mechanistic and interventional investigation.

item.title: REM Sleep Iota Oscillations Across the Lifespan
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Iota oscillations are a newly discovered marker of wakefulness and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. So far, iota in REM sleep has only been reported in the surface electroencephalography (EEG) of a small sample of young adults and in intracranial recordings of epileptic patients. Here, we investigated the presence of these oscillations in a large dataset (N=937) of high-density sleep EEG recordings from individuals 7 to 70 years old. We found that iota spectral peaks during REM sleep were between 25 and 40 Hz, slightly faster than in wake (25-35 Hz). Iota power was significantly associated with REM sleep architecture, increasing with both REM duration and across progressive sleep cycles. Iota peaks were observed in individuals of all ages, although the prevalence decreased gradually with age, from 88% in children to 44% in older adults. Most iota spectral peak properties (frequency, amplitude, timing, topography) likewise shifted with age. The most striking effect, however, was in bandwidth, such that children had narrow iota peaks, older adults had broad iota peaks, and 20-30 year olds could have either. It remains unclear whether narrowband and broadband iota are functionally equivalent. On shorter time scales (< 1 year), iota properties remained stable across measurements. Analyses of a separate dataset of monozygotic and dizygotic twins revealed high heritability of all iota peak properties except bandwidth. Overall, these results establish iota as a genetically determined trait-like marker of REM sleep with unique age-related changes. Iota oscillations open new avenues to investigate the interaction between sleep, genetics, development, and aging.

item.title: Neurodegeneration epicenters: Distinct network mechanisms of dopaminergic treatment in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Neural regeneration research
Abstract Parkinson's disease exhibits heterogeneous spatiotemporal patterns of neurodegeneration. Dopaminergic therapy improves motor symptoms by modulating brain function in affected regions, yet whether the neural mechanisms through which dopaminergic therapy exerts its effects are linked to this heterogeneity of neurodegeneration remains unclear. A connectivity-based epicenter framework combined with spectral dynamic causal modeling was applied to resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 160 drug-naïve Parkinson's disease patients and 174 healthy controls to identify subtype-specific degenerative epicenters and characterize directional interactions among affected regions. Ninety-seven patients additionally underwent an acute levodopa challenge to evaluate how dopaminergic modulation influences these interactions and relates to symptom improvements. Two distinct Parkinson's disease subtypes were identified: subtype 1 was characterized by degenerative epicenters predominantly located in subcortical and cerebellar regions, whereas subtype 2 exhibited epicenters primarily involving cortical regions. Both subtypes exhibited widespread dysregulation of directional interactions among epicenter regions relative to healthy controls. Levodopa treatment partially reversed these network abnormalities in a manner specific to each subtype, notably within cerebellar vermis in subtype 1 and frontal cortex in subtype 2. Symptom improvements were linked to distinct network interactions: in subtype 1, tremor correlated with the thalamus, midbrain nuclei, and cerebellar vermis, whereas bradykinesia primarily involved the cerebellar vermis; in subtype 2, rigidity improvements mapped to frontal cortex and limbic regions, and bradykinesia to limbic regions. These findings suggest that Parkinson's disease involves distinct epicenter networks in each subtype, with widespread directional dysregulation contributing to symptom diversity in patients. Levodopa treatment selectively modulates these network interactions, shedding light on the mechanisms underlying treatment heterogeneity and guiding precision-targeted therapeutic strategies.

item.title: Functional neuroimaging as a tool to understand social determinants of health in cognitive aging and ADRD: a scoping review
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The social, structural, and physical conditions in which individuals live, work, and age, collectively termed social determinants of health (SDOH), are associated with risk of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). Differences in brain function in later life may offer understanding of how SDOH become biologically embedded and confer differential ADRD risk. However, how functional neuroimaging techniques have been used to study SDOH in cognitive aging and ADRD has yet to be systematically characterized. We therefore conducted a scoping review. Three databases were searched, 2,930 articles were screened, and 41 studies were included. Education was the most frequently studied SDOH domain, accounting for 65.9% (k = 27) of studies, followed by economic and occupation (k = 9, 22.0%), social and community (k = 5, 12.2%), food (k = 4, 9.8%), and physical environment (k = 3, 7.3%). Of the 41 studies, five (12.2%) examined multidomain determinants and one study (2.4%) examined three determinants each from different domains. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was most frequently employed (k = 31, 75.6%), followed by electroencephalography (EEG; k = 7, 17.1%), and magnetoencephalography (MEG; k = 4, 9.8%). One study (2.4%) employed a multimodal approach, while none used functional near-infrared spectroscopy. Resting state paradigms (k = 27, 65.9%) outnumbered task-based (k = 14, 34.1%) and most studies were cross-sectional (k = 38, 92.7%). The predominant focus on education, fMRI, and cross-sectional designs highlights many opportunities for future investigation of how SDOH may be associated with later life brain function.

item.title: Problematic social media and gaming use, screen time, and youth mental health and brain structure in the ABCD Study
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
In an increasingly digital age, knowing which kinds of screen use relate to mental health in adolescents could help guide prevention efforts for a vulnerable population. Earlier work has examined this question, but the findings have been difficult to interpret. For instance, most studies measure screen use in hours, while it may be more informative to know whether adolescents have difficulty controlling their use. This is especially important now that adolescents use screens for school, games and contact with friends. Whether these patterns are reflected in the brain also remains largely unexplored. ABCD Study release 7.0 (N=11,860) is well suited to these questions because of its comprehensive profiling across neuroimaging, behavioral and clinical domains. In a preregistered study, we examined how screen time, problematic social media use (SMAQ) and problematic video game use (VGAQ) relate to parent-rated mental health, brain structure and resting-state connectivity. All five confirmatory associations were positive but small (β = 0.051 to 0.173) and remained consistent across several robustness checks. In the same participants, the problematic use scales were more strongly related to attention problems than hours of use were. The association between screen time and anxiety problems was present in male but not female participants. More screen time was associated with slightly smaller putamen and caudate volumes, while resting-state connectivity did not predict SMAQ. In exploratory analyses, SMAQ predicted later attention problems more than the reverse, while for gaming, attention problems predicted later VGAQ more strongly. Most of the association seemed to come from problematic use rather than use time by itself. Overall, the effects were small but consistent, in line with earlier work in the ABCD Study. We hope this analysis can contribute to a better understanding of how social media and gaming relate to adolescent mental health and brain development.

item.title: Personalized Network Mapping Reveals State-Trait Dissociation of Frontoparietal Connectivity in Adolescent Depression: A Longitudinal Study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Prior research linking resting-state networks (RSNs) to adolescent depression has yielded inconsistent findings, partly because group-average templates poorly capture individual brains; a mismatch that may be especially consequential during adolescence, when RSNs grow increasingly heterogeneous across individuals. Using a personalized analysis pipeline in the longitudinal Characterizing Adolescent Trajectories of Depression cohort (38 depressed adolescents [28 female]; ages 14–18; 181 usable scans; avg. participation: 446.18 days), we derived individualized definitions of three canonical depression-related RSNs. Because longitudinal RSN connectivity may reflect both trait-like vulnerability and state-like symptom fluctuation, we used mixed-effects models to decompose connectivity profiles into both components. FPN connectivity showed a significant state-trait dissociation: chronically elevated connectivity predicted greater average symptom burden, while transient increases predicted momentary relief. These effects were undetectable using group-atlas estimates. We suggest FPN connectivity plays a dual, compensatory role in adolescent depression and demonstrate that personalized definitions can reveal clinically meaningful brain–symptom associations.

item.title: Molecularly distinct neurodegeneration shapes the DOPA-dependent dynamic of large-scale brain connectomics in GBA-associated Parkinson’s disease
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract GBA1-associated Parkinson’s disease (GBA1-PD) is a biologically distinct synucleinopathy associated with glucocerebrosidase deficiency, lysosomal dysfunction, and more extensive cortical neurodegeneration. How these molecular abnormalities shape large-scale cortical network dynamics in vivo remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to characterize resting-state EEG functional connectivity and network topology in GBA1-PD and to determine whether GBA1-related molecular pathology is associated with a distinct oscillatory connectome signature and its modulation by dopaminergic treatment. We recorded resting-state EEG in 22 patients with PD (GBA1-PD = 7; LRRK2-PD = 5; sporadic PD = 10) together with 14 age-matched healthy controls. EEG was acquired in OFF and ON dopaminergic states. Functional connectivity was estimated using imaginary coherence (ImCoh) and phase-locking value (PLV) across canonical frequency bands, while network organization was quantified using the graph-theoretical clustering coefficient. Linear mixed-effects models were used to assess therapy- and subtype-specific effects. GBA1-PD exhibited a selective increase in gamma-band clustering coefficient in the ON condition (p = 0.044), which was not observed in LRRK2 or sporadic PD. PLV-based analyses highlighted opposite clustering changes in GBA1 and LRRK2 patients. ImCoh analyses further revealed different therapy-related connectivity changes in genetic and sporadic PD across all frequency bands (all p ≤ 0.0035). Compared with healthy controls, PD was associated with widespread disruption of cortico-cortical connectivity. All significant effects were abolished in surrogate-data analyses, supporting their physiological specificity. Resting-state EEG connectomics may reveal genotype-specific network alterations in GBA1-PD and their modulation by dopaminergic treatment, supporting a relationship between genetic background and large-scale brain network dynamics.

item.title: The network localization and underlying biological basis of heterogeneous structural and functional brain abnormalities in insomnia disorder.
item.description:
Sleep
Insomnia disorder (ID) has become a prevalent sleep disorder worldwide, yet its underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear due to heterogeneous neuroimaging findings and uncertain network localization. We identified brain structural and functional abnormality locations associated with ID from 63 published neuroimaging studies, including 3391 patients and 3433 healthy controls. Using coordinate network mapping combined with a normative connectome database, we mapped these abnormalities to large-scale brain networks of ID across imaging modalities and further decoded them by integrating microscale chemo-architectural, cellular, and cognitive maps. The structural network widely involved the ventral attention (VAN), sensorimotor (SMN), dorsal attention (DAN) and default mode network (DMN); the task-induced network showed a similar but less extensive pattern, predominantly implicating the VAN, DMN, SMN and subcortical network (SCN); in contrast, the resting-state network was largely confined to the left middle frontal gyrus and the bilateral mid-cingulate cortex. Molecular mapping revealed both shared and distinct neurotransmitter signatures across the three networks, involving cholinergic, histaminergic, glutamatergic, noradrenergic, and opioid systems. Cellular decoding showed relatively selective associations of the structural and task-based networks with glial cells and excitatory neurons, whereas the resting-state network exhibited broader associations with glial cells and multiple excitatory and inhibitory neuronal subtypes. Cognitive decoding linked structural and task-based networks to sensorimotor processing and the resting-state network to memory-related functions. Our findings reconcile heterogeneous neuroimaging results and reveal neurobiological substrates of ID from a network perspective, providing a promising biomarker and paving the way for circuit-based precision therapies of ID.

item.title: Resting-state fMRI biomarkers of surgical outcome in temporal lobe epilepsy: Network reorganization, rsfMRI-based prediction models, and cognition - A systematic review.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is a network disorder extending beyond the structurally defined epileptogenic zone. Resting-state functional MRI (rsfMRI) may provide information on brain network alterations relevant to seizure outcome and cognitive risk after epilepsy surgery. We reviewed rsfMRI studies in TLE surgical cohorts to evaluate postoperative network changes, preoperative predictors of seizure outcome, and associations between functional connectivity and cognition. This systematic review followed PRISMA guidelines and was registered in PROSPERO. Fifteen studies were included, comprising 474 TLE patients who underwent resective epilepsy surgery and had at least 1 year of follow-up. Studies were reviewed for patient population, surgery, rsfMRI methodology, networks or regions, outcome definition, postoperative network changes, and cognitive assessments. Despite heterogeneity in patient selection, surgery, rsfMRI analysis, and outcome definition, studies consistently reported reduced DMN-related connectivity in TLE compared with healthy controls. Postoperative functional connectivity in seizure-free patients shifted toward healthy controls patterns in few studies. Preoperative rsfMRI-based prediction models showed promising accuracy for predicting seizure outcome but were generally developed in small cohorts and lacked external validation. Evidence relating rsfMRI to cognition was limited, but implicated thalamic, ascending reticular activating system, and thalamo-occipital connectivity in attention, language, and executive functions. RsfMRI is a promising research biomarker for network-level risk stratification in TLE surgery, particularly for seizure outcome prediction and postoperative network reorganization. Current evidence remains insufficient for clinical implementation. Future studies require larger homogeneous multicenter cohorts, standardized acquisition and preprocessing, consistent outcome definitions, systematic postoperative rsfMRI, neuropsychological assessment, and external validation of prediction models.

item.title: Interpersonal neural synchrony and parent-child behaviors during naturalistic interactions: A systematic review.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Interpersonal neural synchrony (INS), defined as the temporal alignment of neural activity between socially interacting individuals, has been proposed as an index of parent-child interaction quality. However, its relationship with moment-to-moment adjustment of parent-child behavior remains insufficiently understood. This systematic review examined associations between INS and observable behavior during naturalistic parent-child interactions, the factors influencing these associations, and the methods used to investigate them. Following PRISMA guidelines, systematic searches of Scopus, PubMed, and ScienceDirect identified 15 peer-reviewed empirical studies involving children from preschool age to early adolescence. INS-behavior associations were heterogeneous across studies. Higher INS was most consistently associated with mutual engagement, shared positive affect, and supportive parenting, whereas findings concerning reciprocity, responsiveness, and child agency were more context-dependent. Time-resolved analyses further indicated that INS fluctuated in relation to specific behavioral events and revealed temporally asymmetric patterns in which parent or child neural activity preceded that of the interaction partner. However, these patterns do not establish causal directionality and may partly reflect shared exposure to task-related or interactional inputs. Task structure and the availability of direct social cues appeared to shape INS-behavior associations, while parental stress and child social functioning emerged as potential sources of variability in INS. Methodologically, the findings highlight the value of combining micro- and macro-level behavioral coding with time-resolved and directionality-sensitive analyses, alongside stronger controls for spurious synchrony and common inputs. Given the limited number and methodological heterogeneity of available studies, the findings should be regarded as preliminary and primarily hypothesis-generating.

item.title: Responses to unannounced rule changes in adults with developmental disabilities: A community-based pilot study with consumer-grade EEG
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Unannounced changes in rules or environments often precede challenging behavior and limit community participation for adults with developmental disabilities, yet their responses to change have rarely been quantified directly. We recruited adults with developmental disabilities, including those with intellectual disability, at a community day-service center. We administered a probabilistic reversal learning task and recorded resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) via a 14-channel wireless EEG system. Among the 12 adults who performed the task, total errors were comparable across participants (range 31–57), whereas a switch bias index, contrasting perseverative errors (persisting with the previously correct option) with regressive errors (failing to maintain the newly correct option), ranged from −0.96 to +0.91. In the 9 participants included in resting-state EEG analyses, a flatter aperiodic spectrum over the frontal cluster (preregistered, but selected as the focus post hoc) was associated with fewer switches after negative feedback (ρ = .80) and more perseverative errors (ρ = −.72). The preregistered parieto-occipital cluster showed the same direction (ρ = .69, 95% confidence interval [−.11, .97], n = 8), which was opposite to the preregistered prediction. Frontal alpha peak amplitude was associated with accuracy (ρ = .77), and the between-run reliability of resting-state measures was .82–.99. These findings provide preliminary evidence that EEG recorded in community settings can capture individual differences in how people respond to change. Field measurement that includes people with intellectual disability may help extend the evidence base for the Sustainable Development Goals of good health and well-being (SDG 3) and reduced inequalities (SDG 10).

item.title: Hidden Markov Modeling Reveals Altered Functional Network Dynamics in Multiple Sclerosis
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
ABSTRACT Purpose Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a neurodegenerative and demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. Recent evidence suggests that localized gray matter atrophy in MS may be involved in distributed functional brain networks. However, the dynamic trajectory of functional network alterations in MS remains unclear.
